found-body-l01.q: A cell is running anaerobically. Roughly what share of its normal ATP per glucose is it still making?
choices: About 2 of 30-32, roughly 6 percent
About half
About 80 percent, just more slowly
The same amount, but it takes twice as long
found-body-l01.why: Aerobic breakdown yields about 30-32 ATP per glucose; anaerobic stops at 2 and adds lactic acid. That is roughly 6 percent, not a mild slowdown. Half, 80 percent and same-but-slower all underestimate how severe the failure is.

found-body-l01.q: A 61-year-old is found unresponsive with a fingerstick glucose of 38 mg/dL. Why can that number alone explain the coma?
choices: Low sugar thickens blood and slows flow to the brain
Low sugar directly damages the blood-brain barrier
Brain cells run almost entirely on glucose and store almost none
Low sugar makes carbon dioxide build up in brain tissue
found-body-l01.why: Most cells can switch to fat or protein; neurons largely cannot and keep no reserve, so a sugar under 70 mg/dL produces symptoms within minutes. Blood viscosity, barrier damage and CO2 accumulation are not the mechanism.

found-body-l02.q: A patient has a stroke volume of 60 mL and a heart rate of 110. What is the cardiac output?
choices: 1.8 L/min
6.6 L/min
3.6 L/min
11 L/min
found-body-l02.why: Cardiac output is stroke volume times rate: 60 mL x 110 = 6,600 mL/min, or 6.6 L/min. 1.8 and 3.6 come from dividing instead of multiplying; 11 L/min ignores the stroke volume entirely.

found-body-l02.q: An adult has lost roughly 700 mL of blood and the blood pressure is unchanged. What is the best conclusion?
choices: The bleeding has stopped
The bleeding was venous, which does not affect pressure
Blood pressure is the most sensitive early sign of volume loss
About 15 percent loss is usually tolerated with no pressure change, so a normal pressure proves nothing
found-body-l02.why: Roughly 750 mL, about 15 percent of a 5 L volume, is normally absorbed by compensation. A normal pressure is expected here, so it rules nothing out. Venous bleeding drops pressure too once volume is gone, and pressure is a late sign, not a sensitive one.

found-body-l03.q: You find an unresponsive adult with gurgling respirations and no sign of trauma. What is your first action?
choices: Begin chest compressions
Apply a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min
Suction the airway and open it with a head-tilt chin-lift
Check a blood glucose
found-body-l03.why: Gurgling means fluid in the airway, which is an A problem, and A comes first. Oxygen through a flooded airway does not reach alveoli, glucose is a D-level check, and compressions are for a patient without a pulse.

found-body-l03.q: An adult is taking shallow breaths of about 180 mL at 30 per minute. With roughly 150 mL of anatomic dead space, how much of each breath reaches the alveoli?
choices: About 30 mL, so almost no useful ventilation
About 150 mL, which is adequate
About 180 mL, since dead space refills on exhalation
About 330 mL
found-body-l03.why: Subtract dead space from tidal volume: 180 minus 150 leaves 30 mL of alveolar ventilation per breath. The 150 mL is the part that never reaches gas exchange, and it does not add to the breath, so 180 and 330 are both wrong.

found-body-l04.q: An adult trauma patient has a blood pressure of 126/104. What is the pulse pressure and what does it suggest?
choices: 22 mmHg, narrow, suggesting vasoconstriction from early volume loss
22 mmHg, which is within the normal 30-40 mmHg band
104 mmHg, wide, suggesting vasodilation
230 mmHg, which cannot be interpreted
found-body-l04.why: Pulse pressure is systolic minus diastolic: 126 - 104 = 22 mmHg, well under the normal 30-40, and it narrows because clamping arterioles raise the diastolic. It is not normal, it is not wide, and you do not add the two numbers.

found-body-l04.q: Which statement about hypotension in children is correct?
choices: It typically appears after roughly 15 percent volume loss
It is a late, pre-arrest finding, because children hold pressure until about 30-40 percent loss
Children drop their pressure earlier than adults do
Blood pressure is the most reliable perfusion measure in a child
found-body-l04.why: Children clamp vessels and raise rate aggressively, so pressure holds until 30-40 percent of volume is gone and then falls steeply. Judge them on heart rate, skin, capillary refill and alertness, not the cuff.

found-body-l05.q: A 70-year-old with three days of cough has BP 88/44, HR 118, RR 26, and warm flushed skin. Which shock family fits best?
choices: Hypovolemic
Cardiogenic
Distributive
Obstructive
found-body-l05.why: Warm flushed skin with a wide pulse pressure is dilated pipes, and an infectious source makes septic shock the distributive version. Hypovolemic and cardiogenic shock clamp the skin cold and pale; obstructive shock brings distended neck veins.

found-body-l05.q: Why does a large fluid bolus tend to make cardiogenic shock worse?
choices: Fluid dilutes clotting factors and worsens bleeding
The failing pump cannot move the added volume, so it backs up into the lungs
Fluid triggers histamine release and vasodilation
Fluid slows the heart below a useful rate
found-body-l05.why: In cardiogenic shock the tank is full and the pump is weak, so added volume backs up behind the failing ventricle and floods the alveoli. Dilution, histamine and bradycardia are not what the fluid does here.

found-body-l06.q: A patient's kidneys stop filtering. Which system has failed and what accumulates?
choices: Urinary; potassium, acid and fluid
Digestive; undigested food and bile
Endocrine; unused hormones
Lymphatic; tissue fluid only
found-body-l06.why: Filtering blood and balancing water, salt and acid is the urinary system's job, so failure builds potassium, acid and volume. The digestive, endocrine and lymphatic systems have different jobs and different failure patterns.

found-body-l06.q: Failure of which system is most likely to kill within minutes rather than hours?
choices: Digestive
Skeletal
Respiratory
Reproductive
found-body-l06.why: Respiratory, cardiovascular and nervous failure all end at a brain without oxygen in 4-6 minutes, which is why they are the primary assessment. Digestive, skeletal and reproductive failures are measured in hours to years.

found-body-l07.q: A patient has a heart rate of 38 with BP 78/40. Which drug works by blocking the parasympathetic brake on the heart?
choices: Albuterol
Metoprolol
Atropine 0.5 mg IV
Acetylcholine
found-body-l07.why: Atropine blocks acetylcholine at the heart, lifting vagal braking and letting the rate rise. Albuterol works on the sympathetic side at the lung, metoprolol cuts sympathetic drive and would slow the rate further, and acetylcholine is the slowing signal itself.

found-body-l07.q: A patient given albuterol for wheezing now has a heart rate of 118 and shaking hands. What explains it?
choices: An allergic reaction to the drug
The same sympathetic signaling that opens bronchioles also speeds the heart and causes tremor
Developing sepsis
Parasympathetic rebound after the treatment
found-body-l07.why: Albuterol mimics sympathetic signaling, and that wire runs to the heart and skeletal muscle as well as the airway, so tachycardia and tremor are expected side effects. Allergy would bring hives or swelling, sepsis needs an infection, and parasympathetic activity would slow the pulse.

found-body-l08.q: A patient has had profuse diarrhea for four days. Which disturbance is most likely?
choices: Metabolic acidosis from losing bicarbonate-rich intestinal fluid
Metabolic alkalosis from losing acid
Respiratory acidosis from shallow breathing
Respiratory alkalosis from pain
found-body-l08.why: Intestinal fluid is rich in bicarbonate, which is base, so losing it from below leaves the blood acidic. Alkalosis follows vomiting, where the acid is the part being lost. Neither pattern is respiratory, because the CO2 did not cause it.

found-body-l08.q: A septic patient is breathing 30 times a minute. Someone suggests sedating them to slow the rate. Why is that dangerous?
choices: Sedation would mask the fever
The fast rate is clearing lactic acid; suppress it and the pH falls sharply
Sedation raises serum lactate directly
Sedation causes metabolic alkalosis
found-body-l08.why: Tachypnea in a septic patient is respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis. Take the fast dial away and the acid stays with no route out. Sedation does not change temperature readings, does not itself generate lactate, and does not cause alkalosis.

found-body-l09.q: A patient has swollen legs and distended neck veins with clear lung sounds. Which side of the heart is backing up?
choices: Left
Right
Both equally
Neither; this is purely a lung problem
found-body-l09.why: Right-sided backup pushes blood into the body, producing neck vein distension and leg swelling with clear lungs. Left-sided backup floods the alveoli and produces crackles, which are absent here.

found-body-l09.q: Which serum potassium is closest to the level where the heart can stop?
choices: 3.5 mEq/L
4.5 mEq/L
5.0 mEq/L
6.5 mEq/L
found-body-l09.why: A potassium above roughly 6.5 mEq/L can stop the heart, and kidney failure, crush injury and prolonged shock all push it there. 3.5 to 5.0 spans the normal range and is not the danger zone.

found-body-l10.q: A 70 kg adult carries about 42 L of total body water. Roughly how much of that is interstitial, between the cells?
choices: About 3 L
About 11 L
About 28 L
About 42 L
found-body-l10.why: Interstitial fluid is about one quarter of body water, near 11 L. The 3 L figure is plasma inside the vessels and 28 L is the intracellular two thirds, so mixing those up misstates where volume can be lost from.

found-body-l10.q: An adult runs a temperature of 39 C with a respiratory rate of 30 for a full day. What happens to fluid losses you cannot see?
choices: They fall, because the patient is not sweating visibly
They stay at the usual 500-800 mL per day
They rise roughly 10 percent per degree Celsius of fever, and faster breathing adds more
They are cancelled out by water made during metabolism
found-body-l10.why: Insensible loss through skin and breath runs 500-800 mL a day at baseline and climbs about 10 percent per degree C, with tachypnea adding more evaporation. A febrile, fast-breathing patient can run a liter behind without vomiting once.

found-body-l11.q: A patient lies on cold concrete under several blankets and keeps cooling. Which route is still pulling heat away?
choices: Radiation into the air above the blankets
Conduction into the ground
Evaporation of sweat
Convection from wind
found-body-l11.why: Blankets on top slow radiation and convection but do nothing about direct contact with a cold surface underneath, which is conduction. Getting insulation under the patient is the fix. Evaporation is minimal in a cold, dry, non-sweating patient.

found-body-l11.q: A patient with a temperature of 39.2 C has a heart rate of 62 and takes no beta blockers. Why does that combination matter?
choices: It is expected, because fever slows the heart
Relative bradycardia with fever is a real flag, seen with certain infections and with rising intracranial pressure
It means the thermometer reading is wrong
It effectively rules out infection
found-body-l11.why: Fever normally adds about 8-10 beats per minute per degree C, so a pulse in the 60s at 39.2 C is a mismatch worth explaining. It does not rule infection out and the reading is not assumed to be an error.

found-body-l12.q: A clean surgical wound is 10 days old. Which healing phase is it in?
choices: Hemostasis
Inflammation
Proliferation
Remodeling
found-body-l12.why: Proliferation runs about days 3 to 21, building new vessels and collagen and closing the wound. Hemostasis is seconds to minutes, inflammation is days 0 to 3, and remodeling starts around three weeks.

found-body-l12.q: You notice redness spreading outward from a wound. What is the most useful immediate action?
choices: Apply ice for 20 minutes to stop the spread
Mark the border of the redness with a pen and note the time
Give acetaminophen to reduce the swelling
Wrap the limb tightly to contain it
found-body-l12.why: Marking and timing the border converts a vague impression into measurable evidence of how fast infection is advancing. Ice and tight wrapping do not stop spread, and acetaminophen has little anti-inflammatory effect on tissue.

found-body-l13.q: A patient's serum lactate comes back at 2.6 mmol/L. How should that be categorized?
choices: Normal
Intermediate, meaning look hard for a cause
Severe, with markedly higher mortality
Uninterpretable without a blood gas
found-body-l13.why: Under 2.0 mmol/L is normal and 4.0 or above is the severe band. The 2.0 to 3.9 range is intermediate: not reassuring, and it demands a search for the reason tissue is running anaerobically.

found-body-l13.q: A tourniquet has been on a crushed leg for five hours and is about to come off. What is the priority at that moment?
choices: Release it quickly so flow returns as soon as possible
Sit the patient upright to improve breathing
Have cardiac monitoring and a team ready for a potassium surge and arrhythmia
Wait until the patient has eaten something
found-body-l13.why: Reperfusion washes potassium, acid and myoglobin from the starved limb into the central circulation at once, which is how crush syndrome causes sudden arrhythmia or arrest. Speed is not the goal, and posture and food are irrelevant here.

found-body-l14.q: Using 220 minus age, what is the estimated maximum heart rate for a 76-year-old?
found-body-l14.why: 220 minus 76 is 144. The lower ceiling matters because it limits how much an older heart can raise output when stroke volume falls, so the tachycardia you expect in shock may never arrive.

found-body-l14.q: Why does a fall from standing height fracture a hip at 80 but not at 25?
choices: Older adults fall with more force
Bone density falls with age, especially after menopause
Older bone contains more calcium and is more brittle for that reason
Muscle mass increases with age and levers the bone
found-body-l14.why: Loss of bone density is the mechanism, so ordinary forces produce hip, wrist and vertebral fractures. Falls are not harder at 80, bone loses rather than gains calcium, and muscle mass declines with age rather than increasing.

found-body-l15.q: A 3-year-old has inspiratory stridor and suprasternal retractions. What do the retractions tell you?
choices: The child is breathing comfortably
The child is generating large negative pressure to pull air past a narrowing
The obstruction is in the lower airways
The child is hyperventilating from fear
found-body-l15.why: Retractions are visible evidence of hard inspiratory work against resistance, and stridor on the way in localizes that resistance to the upper airway near the larynx. Lower airway narrowing makes noise on exhalation, and anxious hyperventilation does not pull the soft tissue in.

found-body-l15.q: Which vital sign pattern goes with rising pressure inside the skull?
choices: Rising blood pressure with a falling heart rate
Falling blood pressure with a rising heart rate
Both blood pressure and heart rate rising
Both blood pressure and heart rate falling
found-body-l15.why: Cushing's triad is hypertension, bradycardia and irregular breathing: pressure climbs to force blood into the squeezed brain, and baroreceptors answer that pressure by slowing the heart. Falling pressure with tachycardia is the shock pattern, not the intracranial one.

found-body-l16.q: Roughly what steroid exposure is enough to suppress the adrenal axis and put a patient at risk of adrenal crisis?
choices: About prednisone 5 mg daily for more than 3 weeks
A single 5 mg dose
Any inhaled steroid used for one week
Prednisone 5 mg daily for 3 days
found-body-l16.why: Suppression takes sustained exposure, roughly the equivalent of 5 mg of prednisone daily for more than three weeks. Single doses and a few days of treatment do not shut the axis down, so they do not carry the same crisis risk.

found-body-l16.q: A hypotensive patient has not responded to 2 L of fluid. Which question takes five seconds and is the one most often skipped?
choices: Ask about recent travel
Ask whether the patient takes long-term steroids
Ask about family history of hypertension
Ask when they last ate
found-body-l16.why: Adrenal crisis belongs on the short list for fluid-unresponsive hypotension alongside ongoing bleeding, obstruction and pump failure, and a steroid history is the item that is easy to miss. Travel, family history and last meal do not change management in this moment.

found-body-l17.q: A night worker finishes at 07:00 and wants to be asleep by 09:00. When should the last caffeine have been?
choices: By about 03:00, at least 6 hours before sleep
At 06:30, right at the end of the shift
At 08:00, one hour before bed
Timing does not matter as long as the dose is under 200 mg
found-body-l17.why: Caffeine has a half-life near 5 hours, so the working rule is to stop at least 6 hours before intended sleep, which means about 03:00 here. Doses at 06:30 or 08:00 leave most of the drug on board at bedtime, and dose does not remove the timing problem.

found-body-l17.q: Why is a person's own sense of alertness a poor safety check at the end of a long shift?
choices: It is accurate, but people choose to ignore it
Judgment of impairment degrades along with the performance it is supposed to measure
It only applies to people working nights
Alertness ratings are valid only before the shift starts
found-body-l17.why: Reaction time and attention fall before the person notices, and the ability to notice falls with them, which is why fatigued people keep driving. The problem is not willpower, and it is not limited to night workers.

quiz.q: A patient in prolonged shock has a blood pH of 7.22 with no lung disease and normal ventilation. What is producing the acid?
choices: Lactic acid from cells forced onto anaerobic metabolism
Carbonic acid from retained carbon dioxide
Hydrochloric acid absorbed from the stomach
Bicarbonate released by the kidneys
quiz.why: Without enough oxygen, cells stop at 2 ATP per glucose and dump lactic acid, which is why shock produces metabolic acidosis. Retained CO2 would be a respiratory cause and ventilation is normal here; stomach acid stays in the gut; bicarbonate is base, not acid.

quiz.q: Cardiac arrest occurred 8 minutes ago with no bystander CPR. Which tissue has already sustained the most damage?
choices: Skeletal muscle in the legs
The brain
The kidneys
Skin and bone
quiz.why: Brain damage begins at 4-6 minutes without oxygen, so 8 minutes is past that window. Heart muscle tolerates 20-30 minutes, kidneys 30-60, skeletal muscle 2-4 hours, and skin and bone many hours.

quiz.q: A 40-year-old with a panic attack is breathing 38 times a minute and reports numb lips and cramping hands. What has changed in the blood?
choices: Oxygen has fallen far below normal
Glucose has dropped under 70 mg/dL
Carbon dioxide has been blown too low, raising the pH
Lactic acid has accumulated from muscle spasm
quiz.why: CO2 dissolves to form carbonic acid, so blowing it off makes blood alkaline, and alkalosis lowers ionized calcium, which causes tingling and spasm. Oxygen is high, not low, with that rate; hypoglycemia causes confusion and sweating; lactate follows lack of oxygen, not excess ventilation.

quiz.q: A patient has a normal blood volume, a strong heart and clear lungs, but a systolic pressure of 78. Which part of the perfusion system has failed?
choices: The pump
The fluid
The air
The pipes
quiz.why: The same volume in a wider container generates less pressure, so dilated arterioles drop pressure with nothing lost. A failed pump would back fluid into the lungs, a fluid problem needs a source of loss, and the lungs are stated to be clear.

quiz.q: Which bedside finding most directly reflects how well small vessels are delivering blood to tissue?
choices: Capillary refill returning in under 2 seconds
A respiratory rate of 16
A temperature of 37.1 C
Pupils equal and reactive
quiz.why: Capillary refill tests flow through the smallest vessels directly and should return color in under 2 seconds. Respiratory rate reflects ventilation and acid, temperature reflects the thermostat, and pupils reflect neurologic status, none of them peripheral perfusion.

quiz.q: A patient is breathing 20 times a minute with good chest rise, but a pulmonary embolism is blocking flow through much of the lung. Which process is failing?
choices: Ventilation only
Oxygenation, because air is moving but blood is not picking oxygen up
Neither; adequate chest rise rules out both
Ventilation and oxygenation equally
quiz.why: Ventilation is moving air in and out, and that is intact here. Oxygenation is loading oxygen onto blood, and it fails when blood cannot reach ventilated alveoli. Chest rise measures the first process, not the second.

quiz.q: You have opened an unresponsive patient's airway with a jaw-thrust and it is now clear. The chest is not moving. What is the next step?
choices: Check a blood glucose
Apply a cervical collar
Provide positive pressure ventilations
Expose the patient fully to look for injuries
quiz.why: An open airway does nothing if no air is moving, so B follows A immediately. Glucose is a D-level assessment, exposure is E, and a collar does not address the absent breathing.

quiz.q: Why is a jaw-thrust preferred over a head-tilt chin-lift in a patient thrown from a vehicle?
choices: It creates a larger airway opening than a head-tilt
It removes the need for suction
It prevents vomiting during ventilation
It opens the airway without extending the neck, which matters when spine injury is possible
quiz.why: The jaw-thrust lifts the tongue off the posterior pharynx while keeping the cervical spine neutral. It is not a larger opening, it does not clear secretions, and it does nothing to prevent vomiting.

quiz.q: After airway, breathing and circulation are addressed, what does the D step check?
choices: Level of consciousness, pupils, movement and sensation, and blood glucose
Distal pulses in all four limbs only
Complete removal of clothing to find injuries
Drug allergies and current medications
quiz.why: D is disability, meaning the brain: mental status, pupils, motor and sensory function, and a sugar. Full exposure is E, medication history belongs to the secondary assessment, and distal pulses alone are part of circulation.

quiz.q: A 25-year-old with a stab wound has HR 118, BP 122/98, RR 24, cool skin and anxiety. Which single change would most clearly signal that compensation has failed?
choices: A rise in respiratory rate to 28
A fall in systolic pressure to 92
A further rise in heart rate to 130
Capillary refill lengthening from 3 to 4 seconds
quiz.why: Blood pressure is defended last, so a falling systolic means the defenses have been overrun. Faster breathing, a faster pulse and slower refill are all the compensation still working, alarming but not yet failure.

quiz.q: What is the lowest acceptable systolic blood pressure for an 8-year-old using the standard formula?
choices: 70 mmHg
78 mmHg
86 mmHg
96 mmHg
quiz.why: The formula for ages 1 to 10 is 70 plus twice the age in years: 70 + 16 = 86 mmHg. Using 70 alone ignores age, and the other values come from adding the age once or using an adult threshold.

quiz.q: Which mechanism explains why a patient in early shock is pale, cool and sweaty at the same time?
choices: Fever drives sweating while blood pools in the legs
Dehydration dries the skin and cools it by evaporation
Capillaries leak plasma onto the skin surface
Sympathetic activity constricts skin vessels and fires sweat glands together
quiz.why: One sympathetic surge does both: shunting blood away from skin makes it pale and cool while the same signal activates sweat glands. Fever causes warm flushed skin, dehydration does not make skin wet, and plasma does not weep through intact skin.

quiz.q: A 34-year-old is stung by a wasp and within 10 minutes has hives, hoarseness, wheeze and BP 76/40. Why does epinephrine treat several problems at once?
choices: It constricts vessels, opens bronchioles and supports the heart simultaneously
It blocks histamine at its receptor
It expands plasma volume directly
It suppresses the immune response over the next few hours
quiz.why: Epinephrine acts on several sympathetic targets at once, reversing vasodilation, bronchoconstriction and poor cardiac output. Antihistamines block histamine receptors, fluids expand volume, and steroids provide the slower immune suppression; none of those replace epinephrine in the first minutes.

quiz.q: A 60-year-old with a large anterior myocardial infarction has BP 84/60, crackles to mid-lung on both sides and distended neck veins. Which action is most likely to harm this patient?
choices: Applying oxygen to maintain saturation
Giving a rapid 2 L crystalloid bolus
Placing the patient in a position of comfort
Obtaining a 12-lead electrocardiogram
quiz.why: This is cardiogenic shock: the pump cannot move the volume it already has, so a large bolus worsens pulmonary edema. Oxygen, positioning and a 12-lead are appropriate and do not add volume.

quiz.q: Which of these produces shock by physically blocking blood flow rather than by losing volume or losing vessel tone?
choices: Severe gastroenteritis with three days of vomiting
A spinal cord injury at the fifth cervical vertebra
Cardiac tamponade after a chest injury
Bloodstream infection from a urinary source
quiz.why: Blood in the pericardial sac stops the heart from filling, which is obstructive shock, and it does not improve until the fluid is drained. Vomiting is hypovolemic, cord injury is neurogenic and infection is septic, and both of the latter are distributive.

quiz.q: Two hypotensive patients both have a heart rate of 120. One has flat neck veins and the other has distended neck veins with clear lungs. What does that difference tell you?
choices: The distended veins indicate more severe volume loss
Both findings point to hypovolemic shock
Neck veins are not useful once the pressure is low
Flat veins fit volume loss; distended veins with clear lungs fit obstruction
quiz.why: An empty tank collapses the neck veins, while an obstruction upstream of the heart backs blood up and distends them with the lungs still clear. Distension is not a marker of greater blood loss, and the finding remains informative at low pressures.

quiz.q: A patient with untreated diabetes develops a life-threatening emergency over several hours. Which system's control speed does that timeline match?
choices: Endocrine, which works over minutes to days
Nervous, which works in milliseconds
Skeletal, which works over weeks
Integumentary, which works continuously
quiz.why: Hormones travel in blood and act over minutes to days, which is exactly the pace of a diabetic emergency. Nervous control is electrical and near-instant, and the skeletal and integumentary systems are not the source of this crisis.

quiz.q: Which system's job is to drain fluid from tissue and fight infection?
choices: Urinary
Lymphatic and immune
Endocrine
Digestive
quiz.why: The lymphatic and immune system returns interstitial fluid to circulation and mounts the defense against invaders, so sepsis and anaphylaxis are its failures. The urinary system filters blood, the endocrine system signals with hormones, and the digestive system absorbs fuel.

quiz.q: A patient with a severe asthma attack becomes drowsy and hard to rouse. What does this most likely represent?
choices: The patient is finally relaxing as the attack breaks
A separate stroke has occurred
A respiratory problem that has become a nervous system problem
A normal response to the work of breathing
quiz.why: Rising CO2 and falling oxygen reach the brain within minutes, so drowsiness in a struggling asthmatic is impending respiratory failure, not improvement. Fatigue and a coincidental stroke are far less likely than the system chain already in front of you.

quiz.q: A patient with a stimulant overdose has dilated pupils, hot dry skin, HR 150 and agitation. Which description fits?
choices: Parasympathetic excess
Vagal surge
Cholinergic crisis
Sympathetic excess
quiz.why: Wide pupils, a racing pulse and agitation are the sympathetic table read straight down. Parasympathetic excess, vagal surge and cholinergic poisoning all produce the opposite: small pupils, a slow pulse and wet secretions.

quiz.q: A patient strains hard on the toilet, then faints with a heart rate of 44. What happened?
choices: Vagal stimulation slowed the heart and dropped blood pressure
A sudden sympathetic surge overwhelmed the heart
The patient became acutely hypoglycemic
Adrenaline release caused a temporary arrhythmia
quiz.why: Straining fires the vagus nerve, the parasympathetic brake on the heart, dropping rate and pressure enough to cause fainting. A sympathetic surge would speed the heart, and neither low sugar nor adrenaline explains the bradycardia tied to the moment of straining.

quiz.q: A patient found unresponsive in a barn has pinpoint pupils, heavy drooling and tearing, vomiting, wheezing and a heart rate of 48. Which feature best separates this from an opioid overdose?
choices: The pinpoint pupils
The drooling, tearing and wheezing
The depressed level of consciousness
The slow heart rate alone
quiz.why: Both opioids and cholinergic poisoning shrink pupils and depress consciousness. Only the cholinergic picture floods the body with secretions, so drooling, tearing and wheezing are the discriminator. Bradycardia occurs in both.

quiz.q: A patient with a severe COPD exacerbation is retaining carbon dioxide. Which disorder develops and which organ would normally compensate over the following days?
choices: Metabolic acidosis, compensated by the lungs
Metabolic alkalosis, compensated by the kidneys
Respiratory acidosis, compensated by the kidneys retaining bicarbonate
Respiratory alkalosis, compensated by the lungs slowing down
quiz.why: The CO2 caused it, so it is respiratory acidosis, and the only remaining dial is renal bicarbonate retention over a day or two. The lungs cannot compensate for a lung problem, and nothing here loses acid or base to create an alkalosis.

quiz.q: Which blood pH value is inside the normal range?
quiz.why: Normal arterial pH is 7.35 to 7.45, so 7.40 sits in the middle. 7.25 is acidosis, 7.52 is alkalosis, and 6.95 is near the edge of survivable.

quiz.q: A patient with a bowel obstruction has been vomiting for two days and now has a pH of 7.50. Where did the acid go?
choices: Out of the body as gastric hydrochloric acid
Into the urine as ketones
Into the lungs as carbon dioxide
Into the tissues as lactate
quiz.why: Gastric contents have a pH near 1.5 to 3.5, so repeated vomiting throws hydrochloric acid out and leaves the blood relatively alkaline. Ketone loss, CO2 clearance and lactate movement are not what produced this metabolic alkalosis.

quiz.q: A patient with long-standing kidney failure has a potassium of 6.0 mEq/L and appears comfortable, while a previously healthy patient with the same value looks far worse. What explains the difference?
choices: The healthy patient's laboratory value is probably in error
Chronic failure develops slowly and the body adapts around it, while acute change does not allow adaptation
Potassium is only dangerous in patients with normal kidneys
The chronic patient must have been given treatment already
quiz.why: Chronic failure develops over months to years and the body adjusts, which is why chronic patients tolerate numbers that would be a crisis in someone else. Potassium remains dangerous in both, and the difference is adaptation, not a laboratory error.

quiz.q: Which tissue type covers and lines body surfaces?
choices: Connective
Muscle
Epithelial
Nervous
quiz.why: Epithelial tissue covers and lines, from skin surface to the inside of the stomach. Connective tissue binds and supports and includes blood and bone, muscle contracts, and nervous tissue conducts signals.

quiz.q: A patient with liver failure has bruising, a swollen abdomen, yellow skin and new confusion. Which set of lost functions best explains that combination?
choices: Loss of filtration and urine production
Loss of oxygen loading and carbon dioxide clearance
Loss of the pump function of the heart
Loss of clotting factor production, protein production and detoxification
quiz.why: The liver makes clotting factors, makes the proteins that hold fluid in vessels, and clears toxins, so failure gives bleeding, swelling, jaundice and confusion together. The kidney, lung and heart failures listed produce different pictures.

quiz.q: Why is normal saline rather than plain sterile water used to refill the vascular space?
choices: Its particle concentration matches plasma, so it stays extracellular, while plain water would move into cells and burst red cells
Saline is thicker and therefore raises blood pressure faster
Plain water causes an allergic reaction in most patients
Saline carries oxygen and plain water does not
quiz.why: Water follows particles, so an isotonic solution stays where it is put while free water rushes into cells. Saline is not thicker, does not carry oxygen, and plain water's problem is osmotic, not allergic.

quiz.q: An adult weighing 80 kg is making 25 mL of urine an hour. How should that be read?
choices: Normal for this weight
Below the 0.5 mL/kg/hr floor, suggesting inadequate perfusion
Above normal, suggesting fluid overload
Not interpretable without a urine specific gravity
quiz.why: The adult floor is 0.5 mL/kg/hr, which is 40 mL/hr at 80 kg, so 25 mL/hr is low and the kidneys are conserving water because flow is inadequate. It is not high, and the number is actionable without additional laboratory work.

quiz.q: A patient with liver failure has low albumin and swollen legs while being volume depleted inside the vessels. Which mechanism explains the swelling?
choices: Hydrostatic pressure at the arterial end has fallen
The lymphatic vessels have been surgically removed
Low albumin weakens the oncotic pull that normally draws fluid back into the capillary
Sodium has been retained inside the cells
quiz.why: Albumin generates the oncotic pull at the venous end of the capillary, so losing it lets fluid stay in tissue even while the vessels run dry. Falling hydrostatic pressure would reduce swelling, and the other options are not the mechanism here.

quiz.q: A runner collapses in 38 C weather at 95 percent humidity with hot dry skin. Why did the cooling system fail?
choices: Radiation stopped working because the skin was dry
Conduction was blocked by clothing alone
Convection reverses direction above 35 C
Evaporation is the only route left when air is hotter than the body, and high humidity closes it
quiz.why: Above body temperature, radiation, convection and conduction all move heat inward instead of outward, leaving evaporation as the sole exit, and humid air stops sweat from evaporating. That is the setup for heat stroke.

quiz.q: A patient's temperature rises from 37.0 C to 39.0 C. Roughly how much of the heart rate rise can the fever alone account for?
choices: About 16-20 beats per minute
About 2-4 beats per minute
About 40-50 beats per minute
None; fever does not change heart rate
quiz.why: Heart rate rises about 8-10 beats per minute per degree C, so 2 degrees accounts for roughly 16-20 beats. A rise far beyond that needs another explanation, and fever certainly does change the rate.

quiz.q: A hiker is found with a core temperature of 29 C, a barely palpable pulse of 32 and rigid limbs. Which management principle is most important?
choices: Warm the arms and legs first to restore circulation quickly
Handle gently, keep horizontal, remove wet clothing and warm the trunk first
Sit the patient up to improve breathing
Use vigorous limb massage to generate heat
quiz.why: A cold heart fibrillates with rough handling, and warming the limbs first sends cold peripheral blood back to the core, an afterdrop that can trigger arrest. Sitting up and massage both add risk without adding heat where it counts.

quiz.q: A patient with a suspected infection has a respiratory rate of 24 and a systolic pressure of 98 and is oriented and appropriate. Does this meet the qSOFA screen?
choices: No, because the patient is alert
No, because qSOFA requires a temperature criterion
Yes, two criteria are met: respiratory rate 22 or higher and systolic 100 or lower
Yes, but only because the respiratory rate is abnormal
quiz.why: qSOFA needs any two of respiratory rate 22 or higher, altered mental status, and systolic 100 mmHg or lower, and this patient has two. Temperature is a SIRS criterion, not a qSOFA one, and one criterion alone would not be enough.

quiz.q: Why does ibuprofen reduce pain, swelling and fever through a single mechanism?
choices: It blocks histamine at three different receptor types
It suppresses white cell production in the marrow
It constricts local blood vessels at the injury site
It blocks the enzyme that makes prostaglandins, which sensitize nerves, promote swelling and raise the hypothalamic set point
quiz.why: Prostaglandins do all three jobs, so blocking cyclooxygenase addresses all three at once. Ibuprofen is not an antihistamine, does not suppress the marrow, and does not work by vasoconstriction.

quiz.q: A patient has a red, hot, swollen, painful knee that will not bend. Which two mechanisms produce every one of those findings?
choices: Vasodilation and increased capillary permeability
Vasoconstriction and platelet aggregation
Bacterial toxin release and nerve destruction
Muscle spasm and joint effusion alone
quiz.why: Widened vessels bring the redness and heat, leaky capillaries bring the swelling, and the resulting pressure plus prostaglandins and bradykinin bring pain and loss of function. Vasoconstriction would do the opposite, and toxins and spasm are not required for this pattern.

quiz.q: Why is a swollen cell still salvageable while a ruptured one is not?
choices: Swollen cells have already replaced their damaged proteins
Restoring oxygen restarts the sodium-potassium pump and lets the cell pump sodium and water back out, but a ruptured membrane cannot be rebuilt
Swollen cells are protected by surrounding tissue
Rupture only happens in muscle, which regenerates
quiz.why: The swelling comes from a stalled pump, so restoring ATP reverses it. Once the membrane bursts, the contents are gone and the cell dies. Rupture is not limited to muscle, and neighboring tissue offers no protection.

quiz.q: A trauma patient has a base deficit of -9 mmol/L with a blood pressure of 118/72. What does that suggest?
choices: The patient is over-resuscitated with fluid
The value is normal for trauma
Significant hidden bleeding, since a deficit beyond about -6 signals ongoing loss despite a normal pressure
A primary respiratory problem
quiz.why: Base deficit tracks the same tissue oxygen debt as lactate and often moves before the blood pressure does, so beyond about -6 mmol/L it points to occult hemorrhage. It is not a normal finding, not a marker of overfilling, and not respiratory in origin.

quiz.q: A patient with a generalized seizure lasting 3 minutes has a lactate of 5.0 mmol/L twenty minutes later, with normal vital signs and warm dry skin. What is the best interpretation?
choices: Occult septic shock is present and must be treated immediately
The laboratory value should be disregarded
The patient is bleeding internally
Seizure activity itself raises lactate, so this likely needs recheck rather than shock treatment
quiz.why: Vigorous muscle activity drives anaerobic metabolism, and post-seizure lactate typically clears quickly. Lactate is sensitive but not specific, so a repeat value with an otherwise normal examination is the right move rather than assuming shock or ignoring the number.

quiz.q: Why does aging make orthostatic drops in blood pressure more common?
choices: Baroreceptors dull, so the correction to standing is smaller and slower
Blood volume doubles with age
Arteries become more elastic and absorb the pulse
Maximum heart rate rises with age
quiz.why: Blunted baroreceptor sensitivity means the reflex that should restore pressure on standing is weaker and later. Arteries stiffen rather than soften, maximum heart rate falls, and blood volume does not increase.

quiz.q: Roughly how much does glomerular filtration rate decline per year after about age 40?
choices: About 0.1 mL/min
About 1 mL/min
About 10 mL/min
It does not change until age 70
quiz.why: Filtration falls roughly 1 mL/min per year after 40, which is why drugs accumulate and dehydration comes easily in older adults. A 10 mL/min annual loss would produce dialysis-level failure within a decade, and the decline does not wait until 70.

quiz.q: An 86-year-old on warfarin fell and struck her head two weeks ago with no symptoms at the time. She is now slowly more confused. What best explains the delay?
choices: Confusion from the fall is always immediate, so this is unrelated
Anticoagulants prevent bleeding inside the skull
Brain shrinkage stretches bridging veins, so a slow subdural bleed can take days to weeks to declare itself
The skull absorbs blood over two weeks and then releases it
quiz.why: Brain volume falls about 10 percent with age, leaving the bridging veins stretched across a wider gap and prone to slow tearing, and anticoagulation makes it worse rather than protective. Delayed gradual confusion is the classic presentation, not evidence against the mechanism.

quiz.q: An 84-year-old is brought in after a fall, with a temperature of 36.6 C, HR 84, BP 104/62 and new confusion for two days. What should stay high on the list?
choices: Nothing urgent, since the vital signs are normal
Simple mechanical injury from the fall only
Dehydration alone, since older adults drink less
Serious infection, because immunosenescence often removes the fever and the tachycardia
quiz.why: In older adults sepsis commonly presents as a fall, weakness or new confusion with a normal temperature and pulse, so normal-looking numbers do not clear it. Treating this as mechanical injury or simple dehydration is how the infection gets missed.

quiz.q: A 68-year-old with black tarry stools has BP 118/96 and HR 112 with cool skin. Which number should worry you most?
choices: The pulse pressure of 22 mmHg
The systolic of 118
The diastolic of 96
The heart rate of 112 alone
quiz.why: A pulse pressure of 22 mmHg, well under the normal 30-40, shows arterioles clamped down to defend a systolic that still looks reassuring. The systolic is the misleading number, the diastolic in isolation says little, and the tachycardia alone has many causes.

quiz.q: A 32-week pregnant patient laid flat for examination becomes pale with BP 82/48. What is the mechanism?
choices: A sudden amniotic fluid embolism
The uterus compressing the inferior vena cava, cutting blood return to the heart
Vasodilation from lying still
Acute blood loss into the uterus
quiz.why: Supine positioning late in pregnancy lets the uterus compress the vena cava, so preload and therefore cardiac output fall, and rolling the patient onto her left side reverses it within seconds. Embolism and concealed hemorrhage would not resolve with a position change.

quiz.q: A 55-year-old with two hours of chest pressure has HR 44 and BP 88/60 with nausea and sweating. Which pattern does this fit?
choices: Anxiety with a vagal component
Early septic shock
An inferior wall myocardial infarction, where the involved vessel supplies the AV node and carries heavy vagal tone
Neurogenic shock from an undetected spinal injury
quiz.why: Bradycardia with hypotension in a patient with ischemic chest pain is the classic inferior pattern. Sepsis brings fever and warm skin, neurogenic shock requires a cord injury and has no chest pain, and anxiety does not drop the pressure to 88/60.

quiz.q: Two patients are both hypotensive with a heart rate of 124. Patient A has cold clammy skin, patient B has warm flushed skin with a wide pulse pressure. What does the skin tell you?
choices: Patient A is sicker than patient B
Both are hypovolemic and the skin difference is incidental
Patient B is dehydrated and patient A is septic
Patient A fits volume loss with clamped vessels; patient B fits distributive shock with dilated vessels
quiz.why: Cold and clamped means the sympathetic system is defending against a low tank, while warm and dilated with a wide pulse pressure means the pipes themselves have opened. Severity is not what the skin encodes, and the assignment in the third option is reversed.

quiz.q: A bleeding patient stops producing urine before the blood pressure falls. Which hormones explain that?
choices: Aldosterone and antidiuretic hormone, retaining sodium and water
Insulin and glucagon, balancing glucose
Thyroid hormone, raising metabolic rate
Melatonin, tracking the internal clock
quiz.why: Falling renal blood flow triggers renin, producing angiotensin II and aldosterone, and the pituitary adds antidiuretic hormone, so salt and water are held back early. Insulin, thyroid hormone and melatonin have nothing to do with defending volume in hemorrhage.

quiz.q: A 23-year-old motorcyclist is calm and conversational with HR 108, BP 116/92, cool skin and an obvious femur deformity. What is the risk in this presentation?
choices: The calm demeanor confirms the injury is minor
A young patient's strong compensation can look composed until reserve is spent, so under-triage is easy
A pulse of 108 rules out significant bleeding
A narrow pulse pressure is expected after any fracture
quiz.why: The adrenaline surge that sustains blood pressure also sharpens a young patient, so appearance lags physiology, and the first clearly abnormal pressure may be the last warning. The pulse of 108 with a pulse pressure of 24 and cool skin is evidence of shock, not against it.

quiz.q: Cortisol is described as having a permissive effect. What does that mean in practice?
choices: It directly raises blood pressure more than adrenaline does
It permits inflammation to spread
It keeps blood vessels responsive to adrenaline, so without it the pressure response fails
It allows glucose to enter cells without insulin
quiz.why: Cortisol does not raise pressure much by itself; it maintains the vessels' ability to answer catecholamines, which is why adrenal insufficiency produces hypotension that fluids and pressors barely touch. Cortisol suppresses rather than permits inflammation and does not replace insulin.

quiz.q: Which change is expected in a healthy adult's blood pressure overnight?
choices: It rises 10-20 percent
It stays exactly constant
It becomes unmeasurable during slow-wave sleep
It dips 10-20 percent, and failure to dip is associated with higher cardiovascular risk
quiz.why: Normal nocturnal dipping is 10 to 20 percent, and non-dippers carry higher cardiovascular risk. Pressure does not rise overnight, is never flat across 24 hours, and remains measurable throughout sleep.

quiz.q: Someone sleeps only 4 hours instead of 8. Which stage is lost disproportionately and why?
choices: REM, because it is concentrated in the last third of the night
Slow-wave sleep, because it is concentrated in the last third
N1, because it is the lightest stage
All stages equally, since cycles repeat identically
quiz.why: Slow-wave sleep loads the first third of the night and REM the last third, so cutting the night short removes mostly REM. Cycles are not identical across the night, which is exactly why the loss is uneven.

quiz.q: A clinician has been awake for 18 hours. What is the best supported statement about their performance?
choices: Performance is unchanged until about 30 hours awake
Impairment is comparable to a blood alcohol concentration near 0.05 percent
Impairment is comparable to a blood alcohol concentration near 0.20 percent
Only physical strength is affected, not judgment
quiz.why: Seventeen to nineteen hours awake performs like roughly 0.05 percent blood alcohol, and about 24 hours like 0.10 percent. The deficit is in reaction time, attention and error rate, not strength, and it starts well before 30 hours.

quiz.q: A night worker has 25 minutes free and wants to be alert afterward. What is the best use of that time?
choices: A 45-minute nap, extending the break if possible
No nap, since any sleep causes grogginess
A nap of about 20 minutes, which stays out of slow-wave sleep and avoids sleep inertia
A 90-minute nap compressed into the time available
quiz.why: A short nap of about 20 minutes ends before deep slow-wave sleep begins, so waking is clean. A 45-minute nap is likely to break into N3 and produce sleep inertia, a full 90-minute cycle does not fit, and refusing to nap wastes an effective countermeasure.
